title: Checkpoint: Companies and Work
objective: After this level you can explain how businesses make profits, set wages and change with technology.
summary: Coase (1937): firms exist because markets have transaction costs, so managers direct work inside. From pin factories to robots, companies turn costs into revenue and pay wages for labor.

cards.headline: If markets work so well, why do companies exist at all?
cards.body: In theory, you could hire a stranger for every single task, one deal at a time. In 1937, economist Ronald Coase asked why businesses don't simply do that.

cards.headline: The cost of using the market
cards.body: Coase's answer: markets aren't free to use. Every deal means finding out prices and negotiating a separate contract, costs now called transaction costs. A firm cuts them. Instead of a fresh contract for each task, managers direct the work inside. The idea helped earn Coase the 1991 Nobel Prize in economics, and it explains why this chapter's companies exist at all.

events.label: Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations opens with the division of labor
Luddites begin smashing stocking frames near Nottingham
Aron Salomon turns his boot business into a limited company
The Model T falls from $850 to as little as $260
GM recognizes the United Auto Workers; Coase publishes "The Nature of the Firm"
Unimate, the first industrial robot, starts work at General Motors

cards.headline: The chapter through Coase's eyes
cards.body: Look back through Coase's lens. A corporation is a legal person that can own property and sign contracts. An entrepreneur organizes it and carries the risk. Inside, work is directed rather than bargained task by task. Profit is revenue minus total cost, and economies of scale push the cost of each unit down. Wages are the price of the labor it hires.

cards.headline: Chapter 9 complete
learned: Companies are separate legal persons with limited liability
Profit is revenue minus total cost
Scale and specialization cut the cost of each unit
Wages are the price of labor, bargained alone or together
Firms exist because using markets has costs

questions.prompt: According to Coase, what do firms save on by organizing work inside?

options.label: Taxes on the goods they import
options.rationale: Coase was talking about the costs of making deals.

options.label: Transaction costs of using the market
Wages, since staff work without pay
options.rationale: Firms still pay wages; they save on deal-making.

options.label: Advertising, since firms need no ads
options.rationale: Coase's point was about contracts and prices, not ads.

questions.explanation: Using markets means finding prices and negotiating contracts. Firms cut those transaction costs by directing work inside.

questions.prompt: A publisher could hire a freelance editor for every book, or keep editors on staff. By Coase's logic, why keep them on staff?

options.label: Staff editors are always paid less than freelancers
options.rationale: Coase's point is about the cost of making deals, not pay rates.

options.label: The law forbids publishers from hiring freelancers
options.rationale: No such law: the reason is transaction costs.

options.label: Staff editors always work faster on every book
options.rationale: Speed isn't Coase's argument; deal-making costs are.

options.label: It avoids negotiating a new contract for each book

questions.explanation: Coase: every market deal has costs, such as negotiating a separate contract. Staff can simply be directed to the next book.

questions.prompt: From Level 84: as Ford built more and more Model Ts, what happened to the price?

options.label: It fell from $850 to as little as $260
It rose from $260 to $850
It stayed at $850 throughout
options.rationale: It fell as mass production spread costs.

options.label: It fell to $85 by the 1920s

questions.explanation: Economies of scale: mass production cut the cost of each car, and the price fell from $850 to as little as $260.

questions.prompt: From Level 87: what did General Motors agree to when the Flint strike ended in 1937?

options.label: Closing its Flint plants for good
options.rationale: The plants stayed open; GM dealt with the union.

options.label: Replacing the strikers with new workers
options.rationale: Sitting inside made replacing them hard.

options.label: Recognizing the United Auto Workers
Selling the plants to the strikers
options.rationale: GM kept the plants and recognized the union.

questions.explanation: On February 11, 1937, General Motors agreed to recognize the United Auto Workers.

questions.prompt: Which list puts these Chapter 9 moments in order, oldest first?

options.label: Salomon's company → Pin factory → Luddites → Unimate
options.rationale: Smith's pin factory (1776) came more than a century before Salomon (1892).

options.label: Pin factory → Luddites → Salomon's company → Unimate
Luddites → Pin factory → Unimate → Salomon's company
options.rationale: The pin factory (1776) came before the Luddites (1811).

options.label: Pin factory → Salomon's company → Unimate → Luddites
options.rationale: The Luddites (1811) came long before Unimate (1961).

questions.explanation: Smith's pin factory in 1776, the Luddites in 1811, Salomon's company in 1892, Unimate in 1961.
